{{short description|Blackboard used by Albert Einstein on 16 May 1931 lectures at the University of Oxford}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}}
[[File:Einstein blackboard.jpg|300px|thumb|Einstein's Blackboard at the [[History of Science Museum, Oxford|History of Science Museum]] in [[Oxford]]]]
{{Albert Einstein series|expanded=Legacy}}
'''Einstein's Blackboard''' is a [[blackboard]]<ref name="blackboard">{{cite web| url=https://www.mhs.ox.ac.uk/blackboard/ | title=Bye-bye blackboard ... from Einstein and others | publisher=[[History of Science Museum, Oxford]] | location=UK | access-date=24 December 2024 }}</ref> which physicist [[Albert Einstein]] (1879–1955) used on 16 [[May 1931]] during his lectures while visiting the [[University of Oxford]] in England.<ref>{{citation| contribution-url=http://geekatlas.com/photo/einsteins-blackboard-at | section=Einstein's Blackboard at Oxford's Museum of the History of Science | last=Garrett | first=C. | date=June 11, 2009 | url=http://geekatlas.com/ | title=The Geek Atlas | access-date=14 April 2014 }}</ref><ref name="robinson19">{{cite book| first=Andrew | last=Robinson | authorlink=W. Andrew Robinson | title=[[Einstein on the Run]] | chapter=Blackboard Matters | pages=160–166 | publisher=[[Yale University Press]] | date=2019 | isbn=978-0-300-23476-3 }}</ref><ref name="robinson24">{{cite book| first=Andrew | last=Robinson | author-link=W. Andrew Robinson | title=Einstein in Oxford | chapter=Preface: Einstein's Oxford Blackboard | date=2024 | publisher=[[Bodleian Library Publishing]] | isbn=978-1-85124-638-0 | pages=8–14 }}</ref> The blackboard is in the collection of the History of Science Museum in [[Oxford]].<ref>{{cite web| title=Einstein's Blackboard – in Oxford's Museum of the History of Science | first=Jim | last=Bennett | date=14 December 2010 | authorlink=Jim Bennett (historian) | url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ByXHaNBqi3E | publisher=[[YouTube]] | access-date=14 April 2014 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.hsm.ox.ac.uk/blackboard-used-by-albert-einstein | title=Blackboard Used by Albert Einstein: Relic of a secular saint | publisher=History of Science Museum, Oxford | location=UK | access-date=24 December 2024 }}</ref> The equations in the blackboard are related to the cosmological model known as [[Friedmann–Einstein universe]].

==Overview==
The lecture in which the blackboard was used was the second of three, delivered at [[Rhodes House]] in [[South Parks Road]]. Einstein's visit to give the Rhodes Lectures, and also to receive an honorary [[Doctor of Science]] degree from Oxford University on 23 May 1931, was hosted by the physicist [[Frederick Lindemann, 1st Viscount Cherwell|Frederick Lindemann]].<ref>{{cite book| first=Ronald W. | last=Clark | authorlink=Ronald W. Clark | title=The Life and Times: Einstein – An Illustrated Biography | year=1984 | pages=255–256 | publisher=Wings Books | location=New York | isbn=0-517-14718-1 }}</ref> Einstein's first lecture was on [[Theory of relativity|relativity]], the second on [[cosmology]], and the third on [[unified field theory]]. All the lectures were delivered in [[German language|German]]. A brief report of the second lecture was given in ''[[The Times]]''<ref>''[[The Times]]'', 18 May 1931.</ref> and in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]''.<ref>{{cite journal| title=Our Astronomical Column | journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] | date=1931 | volume=127 | issue=3212 | page=790 |doi=10.1038/127794a0 | bibcode=1931Natur.127..794. }}</ref> A summary of all three lectures can be found in the Archives of the Oxford Museum for the History of Science.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.mhs.ox.ac.uk/collections/search/display-narrative/?irn=9738&index=3 | title=Printed Pamphlet Accompanying The Rhodes Lectures, Oxford | date=1931 | first=Albert | last=Einstein | authorlink=Albert Einstein | publisher=[[Museum of the History of Science, Oxford]] | location=UK }}</ref>

The blackboard was rescued with another board by dons (including the chemist [[E. J. Bowen]], zoologist [[Gavin de Beer]], and historian of science [[Robert Gunther]]<ref name="fox18">{{cite journal| first=Robert | last=Fox | authorlink=Robert Fox (historian) | title=Einstein in Oxford | journal=[[Notes and Records]] | volume=72 | issue=3 | pages=293–318 | publisher=[[The Royal Society]] | date=23 May 2018 | doi=10.1098/rsnr.2018.0002 | doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite book| first=A. E. | last=Gunther | series=Early Science in Oxford | volume=XV | title=Robert T. Gunther | publisher=[[Oxford University Press|Oxford]] | date=1967 | pages=250, 436 }}</ref><ref name="robinson19" />) and formally donated by the [[Warden (college)|Warden]] of Rhodes House, Sir [[Francis James Wylie]].<ref>{{citation| title=Einstein's Blackboard | work=Label in gallery | publisher=History of Science Museum, Oxford | location=UK | date=2014 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news| title=Einstein's Blackboard | first=Mark | last=Callaghan | date=20 May 2011 | work=[[The Oxford Student]] }}</ref> The writing on the blackboard, although [[ephemeral]] in nature, is of historic interest because the equations displayed are taken from a model of the universe proposed by Einstein in May 1931 known as [[Friedmann–Einstein universe]].<ref name="einstein-1931">Einstein, A. 1931. Zum kosmologischen Problem der allgemeinen Relativitätstheorie Sitzungsb.König. Preuss. Akad. 235-237</ref><ref name="cor-2013">O’Raifeartaigh, C. and McCann, B. (2014) ‘Einstein’s cosmic model of 1931 revisited: an analysis and translation of a forgotten model of the universe’.Eur. Phys. J. (H) 39 (1), pp. 63–85. [https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.2192 Physics ArXiv preprint].</ref><ref name="Kragh-2013">Kragh, H. (2013). ‘Cyclic models of the relativistic universe: the early history’. [https://arxiv.org/abs/1308.0932 Physics ArXiv 1308.0932].</ref> The last three lines on the blackboard are estimates of the density of matter in the universe ''ρ'', the radius of the universe ''P''  and the timespan ''t'' of the expansion of the universe respectively. It has recently been shown that these estimates contain a systematic numerical error.<ref name="cor-2013"/>

The blackboard is considered a "mutant" object or artefact because it no longer serves the philosophical purpose of a blackboard, namely temporary information storage. By keeping Einstein's writings on it for ever, the blackboard became something else and can only regain to its original purpose by being wiped.<ref>{{citation| contribution-url=http://jfgauvin2008.wordpress.com/2009/03/09/einsteins-blackboard/ | section=Einstein’s Blackboard as a Mutant Object | first=Jean-Francois | last=Gauvin | date=9 March 2009 | url=http://jfgauvin2008.wordpress.com/ | title=Carrière et vie professionnelle | publisher=[[WordPress]] | access-date=14 May 2014 }}</ref><ref>{{citation| contribution-url=http://scientificobjects.mpiwg-berlin.mpg.de/scientificobjectsPublic/index/Archive/Wandering-Seminar-Archive/Objects-Wandering-Seminar/20.html | section=Einstein’s Blackboard as a Mutant Artefact | url=http://scientificobjects.mpiwg-berlin.mpg.de/ | title=History of Scientific Objects | location=Germany | publisher=International Max Planck Research Network | access-date=14 May 2014 }}</ref><ref>{{citation| contribution-url=http://pietrow.net/relics/#Einsteins_blackboard | section=Einstein’s Blackboard | title=Einstein's Blackboard in Oxford | access-date=14 January 2019 }}</ref> A second blackboard used by Einstein during the lecture was also donated to the museum, but was accidentally wiped clean by a museum cleaner.<ref>{{citation| first=Albert | last=Einstein | title=Einstein Blackboard No.2, 1931 | work=MHS Collection Database Search | publisher=History of Science Museum, Oxford | location=UK | date=1931 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal  | title = Investigations into the origin of Einstein's Sink | journal = Studium | year = 2019 | volume = 11 | issue = 4 | pages = 260–268 | doi=10.18352/studium.10183| last1 = Pietrow | first1 = Alexander G.M. | arxiv = 1905.09022 | bibcode = 2019Studi..11E...1P | doi-access = free }}</ref>

Einstein returned to Oxford again in 1932 and 1933 before he settled at [[Princeton University]] in the United States for the rest of his life.<ref>{{cite book| first=Andrew | last=Robinson | authorlink=W. Andrew Robinson | title=Einstein: A Hundred Years of Relativity | year=2005 | page=96 | publisher=[[Palazzo Editions]] | isbn=0-9545103-4-8 }}</ref>

==Content==
The blackboard reads

{{math proof | title=Blackboard|
:<math>D=\frac{1}{c}\frac{1}{\ell}\frac{\mathrm d \ell}{\mathrm dt}=\frac{1}{c}\frac{1}{P}\frac{\mathrm d P}{\mathrm d t}</math>

{{NumBlk|:|<math>D^2=\frac{1}{P^2}\frac{P_0-P}{P}\sim  \frac{1}{P}</math>|1a}}

{{NumBlk|:|<math>D^2=\frac{\kappa\rho}{3}\frac{P_0-P}{P_0}\sim  \kappa \rho</math>|2a}}

:<math>D^2\sim 10^{-53}</math>

:<math>\rho \sim 10^{-26}</math>

:<math>P \sim 10^{8}\;\text{l.y.}</math>

:<math>t \sim 10^{10} (10^{11})\;\text{y}</math>
}}
where the variables refer to Friedmann–Einstein universe, where  <math>D</math> is defined in the equations, <math>c</math> is the [[speed of light]], <math>\ell</math> is the [[scale factor]], <math>P</math>  is the radius of the universe (measured in light years) and <math>P_0</math> its maximal value, <math>\rho</math> is the mean density of matter, <math>t</math> is time and the age of the universe (last line, measured in years), and <math>\kappa</math> is the [[Einstein gravitational constant|Einstein's gravitational constant]].

===Analysis===
In 2013, it was pointed out<ref name="cor-2013"/><ref name="Kragh-2013"/><ref name="ORaifeartaigh15">{{cite web|last=O'Raifeartaigh|first=C.|title=Einstein's blackboard and the Friedman-Einstein model of the cosmos|url=https://coraifeartaigh.wordpress.com/2015/12/22/einsteins-blackboard/|website=Antimatter|publisher=[[WordPress]]|date=22 December 2015|access-date=31 December 2015}}</ref> that the equations on the Oxford blackboard had been taken directly from a key paper on relativistic cosmology written by Einstein in April 1931 and published in the Proceedings of the Royal Prussian Academy of Science on 9 May that year.<ref name="einstein-1931" /> The paper, known as the Friedmann–Einstein universe, is of historic significance because it constituted the first scientific publication in which Einstein embraced the possibility of a cosmos of time-varying radius. In the paper,<ref name="einstein-1931" /> Einstein adopts [[Alexander Friedmann]]'s 1922 analysis<ref>Friedman, A. 1922. Über die Krümmung des Raumes. Zeit. Physik. 10 : 377-386</ref> of relativistic models of a universe of time-varying radius and positive curvature, but sets the [[cosmological constant]] to zero, declaring it redundant, predicting a universe that expands and contracts over time. With the use of [[Edwin Hubble]]'s observations<ref>{{cite journal |last=Hubble |first=Edwin |date=1929-03-15 |title=A relation between distance and radial velocity among extra-galactic nebulae |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=15 |issue=3 |pages=168–173 |doi=10.1073/pnas.15.3.168|pmid=16577160 |pmc=522427 |bibcode=1929PNAS...15..168H |doi-access=free }}</ref> of a linear redshift/distance relation for the spiral nebulae, Einstein extracts from his model estimates of ''ρ'' ~ 10<sup>−26</sup> g/cm<sup>3</sup>, ''P'' ~ 10<sup>8</sup> light-years and ''t'' ~ 10<sup>10</sup> years for the density of matter, the radius of the cosmos and the timespan of the cosmic expansion respectively. These values are displayed in the last three lines on the Oxford blackboard (although the units of measurement are not specifically stated for the density estimate, [[Centimetre–gram–second system of units|cgs]] units are implied by the other calculations).

==Error==
It has also been noted<ref name="cor-2013"/><ref name="ORaifeartaigh15" /> that the numerical estimates of cosmic parameters in Einstein's 1931 paper – and on the blackboard – contain a systematic error. Analysis of the 1931 paper shows that, given the contemporaneous Hubble constant of 500&nbsp;km s<sup>−1</sup>Mpc<sup>−1</sup>, Einstein's estimates of cosmic density, radius and timespan should have been ''ρ'' ~ 10<sup>−28</sup> g/cm<sup>3</sup>, ''P'' ~ 10<sup>8</sup> light-years and ''t'' ~ 10<sup>9</sup> years respectively. One line on the blackboard, not included in the published paper, makes the nature of Einstein's error clear. In the fourth line on the blackboard, Einstein obtains a value of 10<sup>−53</sup> cm<sup>−2</sup> for the quantity ''D''<sup>2</sup>, defined in the top line of the blackboard as<blockquote><math>D=\frac{1}{c}\frac{1}{P}\frac{\mathrm d P}{\mathrm d t}</math>,</blockquote>i.e., the [[Hubble constant]] divided by the speed of light. Simple calculation shows that the contemporaneous value of the Hubble constant in fact implied a value of ''D''<sup>2</sup> ~ 10<sup>−55</sup> cm<sup>−2</sup> (or 10<sup>−51</sup> m<sup>−2</sup>) for this quantity. It appears that Einstein stumbled in converting [[Parsec|megaparsecs]] to cm, giving a density of matter that was too high by a factor of a hundred, a cosmic radius that was too low by a factor of ten, and a timespan for the expansion that was too high by a factor of ten.<ref name="cor-2013" /> These errors were corrected in a later review of relativistic cosmology written by Einstein in 1945.<ref>{{cite book| last=Einstein | first=A. | date=1945 | chapter=Appendix: On the cosmological problem | title=The Meaning of Relativity | publisher=[[Princeton University Press]] | location=Princeton | edition=2nd }}</ref>

==Nottingham blackboard==
A blackboard used by Einstein in a public lecture at the [[University of Nottingham]] on 6 June 1930 was also preserved after the lecture and is part of the university's archives.<ref>Charlotte Anscombe, [http://blogs.nottingham.ac.uk/newsroom/2015/06/05/remembering-whenalbert-einstein-visited-the-university-and-was-late/ 'Remembering when ... Albert Einstein visited the university - and was late!'] (University of Nottingham, 5 June 2015)</ref>
The blackboard is presently on display inside a protective frame and screen, within the university's Department of Physics and Astronomy. During term time it can be seen by academics and students within the classroom it's in. Visitors to campus can see it on display during university open days, if they take a tour of the department.
[[File:University_of_Nottingham_Physics_and_Astronomy_department's_"Einstein's_Blackboard".png|thumb|Einstein's Blackboard at the University of Nottingham, department of physics and astronomy.]]
{{math proof | title=Blackboard (Nottingham)|
:<math>\nearrow {\underline{h_{\mu}{}^\nu} \atop \underline{\underline{\phi_\nu}dx_\nu} }  \;\;\;  {{{}^{\nearrow}\sum dx_\nu^2=0 }\atop{ \sum \underline{g_{\mu\nu}}dx_\mu dx_\nu=0 } }_{ds^2} </math>
Einleitende Bemerkung<br>
Begriff des Körpers<br>
Räumliche Beziehungen der Körper<br>
Raumbegriff in der Mathematik (Deskartes)<br>
Newtons Raum<br>
Feldbegriff (Faraday Maxwells Lorentz)<br>
Spezielle Relativitätstheorie<br>
Allgemeine R.Th. und  Geometrie<br>
Einheitliche Feldtheorie{{Quad}}{{Rotate text| -40|A. Einstein<br>{{Quad}}{{Quad}}6. VI 30.}}
}}When translated, it reads as a table of contents in English:

* Introductory remarks
* Concept of the body
* Special relations between bodies
* Concept of space in mathematics (by [[René Descartes]])
* Newtonian space
* Concept of the field (by [[Michael Faraday]], [[James Clerk Maxwell]] and [[Hendrik Lorentz]])
* Special relativity theory
* General theory of relativity and geometry
* [[Unified field theory]]
